![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14133250/assets/b2f6d99ad589e6f93ddbaf260c75b53c265dfdaa1085d69cece362038f6e251e.png)

Consider the vector field $F=⟨0,\,{z}^{2},\,y⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of the solid onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\bbox[3pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAA}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
question.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=0$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper plane ${S}_{1}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is upward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨0,{z}^{2},y⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower hemisphere ${S}_{2}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=\frac{y}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=0,\,Q={z}^{2}=1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,R=y.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂h}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-0\cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-(1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot \frac{y}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}-y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}y\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}-y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$
